extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and beginner fiction writers (including NaNoWriMo participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for drafting and revising a novel's opening chapter so it hooks readers: what to include, what to avoid, and when to postpone polishing until later drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the First Chapter Last
rubrics_metrics.description: DO Write your First Chapter Last
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stop agonizing over the opening—sketch it and move on to write the rest of the story. In the first draft you're writing for yourself; edit later for the reader. The opening often changes dramatically during drafting; you may cut or move the original first chapter. For NaNoWriMo participants this prevents wasting the month on endless revision. Sneak backstory into later chapters rather than dumping it all up front; many teachers find student novels often truly begin several chapters in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid opening with death or false starts
rubrics_metrics.description: DON’T Open with Death or Trick Your Reader with False Starts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening with a death is clichéd and can feel like a cheap provocation—agents and readers may be turned off. Avoid dream openings and scenes that appear to be the main story only to reveal they concerned different characters or times (false starts). Such openings leave readers feeling cheated and are a common reason readers stop reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce the Protagonist in the First Chapter
rubrics_metrics.description: DO Introduce the Protagonist in the First Chapter
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a scene involving the main character (generally one protagonist unless it's an intentional saga). You don't need exhaustive physical description; give enough (gender, approximate age/status) and, most importantly, the character's emotions in the scene so readers can empathize. Showing an identifiable, sympathetic reaction (e.g., embarrassment, fear) helps readers care and invest in the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t start with unanchored or reader-feeder dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: DON’T Start with Dialogue, Especially Reader-Feeder
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid opening with unanchored dialogue because readers don't yet know who is speaking, where they are, or why to care. Also avoid 'as-you-know' dialogue that dumps exposition. Dialogue should reveal character and advance the scene, not provide clumsy background information for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include interaction with more than one character early
rubrics_metrics.description: DO Put More than One Character in your First Chapter
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standalone introspection scenes ('Robinson Crusoe' or alarm-clock wakeup openers) often feel like 'throat-clearing' with no story action. Scenes with at least two characters create interaction and conflict; if a scene has one person only, ensure they're dealing with significant obstacles to keep interest. Introducing multiple characters (even briefly mentioned) can make scenes feel natural, but avoid excessive, confusing group dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid crowds and multiple concurrent battles/characters
rubrics_metrics.description: DON’T Put in too Many, Either: Avoid Crowds and Battles
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting 'in media res' by dumping the reader into a sprawling battle or crowd can prevent emotional focus—readers won't know whom to root for. Keep the opening scene manageable and centered on the protagonist (or a single focused player) so the reader can form an attachment. If you must open in a large-scale event, choose a narrow, character-focused slice of that event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish time/place succinctly
rubrics_metrics.description: DO Let Us Know Where We Are
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers need to know the basic setting (planet/historical time period) without being bogged down by excessive worldbuilding. It's acceptable to give straightforward, compact exposition to orient the reader (Jeffrey Eugenides example). In SF/Fantasy, limit first-chapter descriptions to essentials that let the reader picture the immediate scene without slowing the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conflict that creates tension, not just violence
rubrics_metrics.description: DON’T Equate Conflict with Violence: Create Real Tension that Propels the Story
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict doesn't have to be physical; small domestic or interpersonal conflicts can generate escalating tension that propels the story. The opening should present a conflict that raises further questions and ties into a larger underlying tension or problem, so readers keep reading after the immediate scene resolves (e.g., Hunger Games' selection fear vs. larger dystopian conflict).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show what the protagonist wants early
rubrics_metrics.description: DO Let us Know What the Protagonist Wants
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear what the main character wants in the immediate scene and, preferably, what their overarching goal will be. The ultimate goal may not be fully revealed in chapter one, but readers should see a present objective that points toward the larger stakes—this orients readers and creates narrative drive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overwrought, purely lyrical openings without story
rubrics_metrics.description: DON’T Take Your Reader on a Nature Walk
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the 'MFA opener' that lavishly describes setting and sensory detail without introducing characters or tension. Lush prose has its place, but in the first chapter keep description lean and use a few bold strokes to establish tone/theme (William Gibson quote as example). Prioritize story/action over poetic description until the reader is invested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin the story (not just scene-setting) immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern readers expect the story to start on page one
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a rigid rule, contemporary readers generally want the story to begin right away rather than spending pages on preliminaries. Use the opening to initiate narrative action or conflict so readers are engaged from the start; you can always refine and relocate the original opening during revision.
